slides.say: An isosceles triangle A B C is inscribed in a circle with center O, and A B equals A C. Given: angle B A C is fifty-six degrees. What is angle A B O?
Angle A B O is the angle marked x, at B, between B A and the radius B O. [short pause] We'll solve it in two different ways. Let's start with the math way.
at: Angle A B O is the angle marked x

slides.say: Angle B A C is an inscribed angle, and it intercepts the arc B C. Angle B O C is a central angle, and it intercepts the same arc.
at: it intercepts the arc B C

slides.say: Remember, a central angle is twice the inscribed angle on the same arc. So angle B O C is two times fifty-six, which is one hundred twelve.
at: So angle B O C is two times

slides.say: Now look at triangle B O C. O B and O C are both radii, so they're equal, and the triangle is isosceles. This time the top angle is one hundred twelve, not sixty, so it isn't equilateral.
at: Now look at triangle B O C
O B and O C are both radii

slides.say: The two base angles share one hundred eighty minus one hundred twelve, which is sixty-eight. Half of sixty-eight is thirty-four. So angle O B C is thirty-four, and so is angle O C B.
at: So angle O B C is thirty-four

slides.say: Careful, thirty-four is angle O B C, not our x. It's choice number two, and it's a trap if you stop here.
[pause] Now let's use the given we haven't used yet. A B equals A C, so triangle A B C is isosceles, and its base angles, at B and at C, are equal.
at: A B equals A C, so triangle

slides.say: The top angle is fifty-six. So the angles at B and C share one hundred eighty minus fifty-six, which is one hundred twenty-four. Half of one hundred twenty-four is sixty-two. So the whole angle A B C is sixty-two.
at: So the angles at B and C share
So the whole angle A B C

slides.say: Let's look closely at the angle at B. The whole angle is sixty-two. The part next to B C, angle O B C, is thirty-four. So x is what's left. Sixty-two minus thirty-four is twenty-eight. Choice number one is our answer. Notice that sixty-two, choice number three, is the whole angle, not x.
at: Let's look closely at the angle at B
Choice number one is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now let's solve it by Understanding, with symmetry. We add one helper line, the radius O A. Then we can use equal radii and symmetry, instead of finding the whole angle at B.
at: Now let's solve it by Understanding

slides.say: From the center O, let's draw a radius to the vertex A.

Now fold the figure along the line through A and the midpoint of B C. The fold swaps B and C. A B is equal to A C, so A stays where it is. And O B is equal to O C, so the center O is on that fold line too. So the radius O A lies right on the fold.
at: fold the figure along the line

slides.say: The fold also swaps the two halves of the angle at A. So O A cuts the angle at A into two equal parts. Fifty-six divided by two is twenty-eight, so we get twenty-eight and twenty-eight.

Now look at triangle A O B. O A and O B are both radii, so it's isosceles too, and its base angles are equal. So x is equal to angle O A B, which is twenty-eight. Choice number one again. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: Now look at triangle A O B
O A and O B are both radii
